newsitem.title: UK: Heart disease still not being prevented - conference.
newsitem.headline: Heart disease still not being prevented - conference.

text.p: Doctors and patients alike are still failing to prevent deaths from heart attacks, despite strong evidence that both drugs and lifestyle changes can have dramatic effects, British experts said on Tuesday.
Patients are resistant to change, doctors are reluctant to overcome old prejudices, and some of the drugs are expensive, delegates to a conference on clinical cardiology were told.
"Patients don't respond well to health messages," Stuart Cobbe, an expert on primary prevention at the University of Glasgow, told the Royal College of Physicians conference.
"If you're living in a housing estate and unemployed and unemployable after age 40, you're not going to take kindly to being told to eat more lean meat and sun-dried tomatoes."
David Wood of the National Heart and Lung Institute said doctors were also to blame. Prescribing drugs was easier than counselling on diet.
"One of the reasons why these dietary data are not widely known in the cardiological community is because they are not in the form of a pill," he said.

But Cobbe cited several recent studies that show even if people refused to eat less fat, more vegetables and exercise more -- all shown to reduce risk of heart disease -- drugs could still be used to help them.
"In the last two to three years in the field of lipid reduction, we at last have convincing clinical trials which give us hope of reducing the incidence and progression of heart disease," Cobbe said.
For instance, drugs to lower cholesterol such as simvastatin (Merck's Zocor) reduces overall mortality and even death from stroke.
"We can certainly prevent coronary events and coronary deaths with statins," Cobbe said. Such drugs also helped people who had already had heart disease, said Wood.
Yet a Europe-wide study showed that between 40 and 50 percent of those at risk were not getting their blood cholesterol lowered.

Cobbe said this was due to highly publicised studies linking the lowering of cholesterol with a raised increase of other deaths, notably suicide. He said studies since had cleared up the discrepancy and shown that it was safe to lower cholesterol, but it took time for the message to get through.
"The problem is you are trying to change the habits of a professional lifetime," he said. In addition, the drugs could be expensive, depending on who was treated.
Up to 40 percent of all men in Scotland, which has one of the world's highest rates of heart disease, have high levels of cholesterol. Treating all of them is "far beyond our means," Cobbe said.
But careful targeting of those at the highest risk, such as smokers with high blood pressure and cholesterol, would cost less and produce marked results, Cobbe predicted.
The Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study Group reported in January that it cost less to give patients the cholesterol lowering drug than to treat them for later heart disease.
